Echale Fuego
notes: “we're going to play song from what to say which is Echale Fuego Echale Fuego”
Track 2 on 'Tequila, Sangre y Fuego' (2007), the ARIA-nominated album by Sydney Afro-Colombian band Watussi.

transcripts.text: Yes, yes, you are listening to FBi Radio 94.5 and this is Mi Gente, My People and today we've got a very special guest who goes by the name of Cayman Jimenez and we will be chatting to Cayman about a Myrtle Tribe and celebrating the incredible milestone of 10 years with the release of their third LP, Golden Roots. For those who may not know, Amaru Tribe is a five-piece Afro-Colombian polktronic, four-piece, led by the brains behind the project Kaimen Jimenez. Kaimen, welcome to me and to my people. It's a pleasure to have you here and we're excited to celebrate this incredible achievement with you. Thank you, Paulo, and hello to everyone listening. Of course, everyone's listening, don't worry. and let's begin you came from colombia bogota uh barranquilla in bogota barranquilla i was living in bogota when i was when i came before and how old were you before you come to a show i was 22 22 okay grown man young adult yes um tell us about that journey and how did you find yourself here and where did your love for music begin yeah well I um that's three different questions for different times but yeah I came here to initially to study music production I was very passionate about engineers doing sound and that's kind of like what I thought that I wanted to do and I still do it um but through that process of recording and learning how to record I I ended up recording my own music that I always had inside, ideas, but I never had the technology. At that point, it wasn't as easy to get, you know. Around the early 2000s? That's right. It wasn't accessible at all. No, exactly. To have a multi-track wasn't something that you would have straight away, you know. And through that, I learned to record my own songs. And also, while I was in Sydney, which is where I initially arrived to Australia, I ended up planning parties and then sometimes they would invite me to play at a cafe or restaurant. I started to make money that way and decided to give it a go and start making my life by performing. Beautiful. And when you first started your musical journey here in Australia, what was the scene like? I guess that it was a very different scene of what it is now. I mean, the genre of salsa was super popular. I mean, it still is, and I love salsa. Actually, in Sydney, I ended up dancing in some of those salsa bars and going into salsa competition. I love dancing salsa as well. But I also felt like there was so many things happening in Latin America in terms of latin rock and latin music alternative new music that had not arrived to australia yet and so i think that's what's something that kind of inspired me and motivated me to to do something different here beautiful um so you've been building building an alternate latin music community here basically you know so like you you worked like saying with salsa which was bit mainstream so there was a lot of uh let's say interest in that you know but then doing the latin rock you had a group before that which was called yeah my first uh proper project here in australia was called what to see what to see and which had a great success was kind of uh i think a wonderful band that had a lot of love from the community we had a bit of success with the nomination to the areas and tour around Australia, Japan, Korea, many places. And, you know, I got to meet so many, actually got to discover Australia touring with that band. So it was something that really was part of my history here of getting to know the Australian local scene and rediscovering myself as an artist. and uh what was that experience like from coming from colombia and you know just not necessarily wanting to be an artist but falling into that you know like you're the lead singer you know you're out there you know you have that energy you know not not many artists really can do that you know like how was that experience for you i guess it it came in almost natural because i um In Colombia, I did have some experience playing with bands, but I was kind of like backing guitarist and backing vocals of a ska punk band in Bogota, which is called La Brigada. La Brigada. But from those experiences, that was like a very underground scene. It was like we'll play at somebody's garage or somebody's abandoned house. And it was like... DIY. Yeah, this is kind of like... do-it-yourself punk scene. And from those years, I really learned the importance of the energy, of reading the energy of people and, you know, not making too much importance and just, like, give yourself to the audience as well. So I think that kind of came in naturally later on when I performed with Wattusi. but not just that I think that also through the years I learned that my years in Barranquilla experiencing carnival music really kind of flux and mix with that energy too because it was like people in the Caribbean are really spontaneous and it's just about having fun no matter what and that's kind of the blend of what I kind of impersonated on stage that kind of easy going of when my dad would celebrate New Year's or would be in a house party he would be like making everybody dance and standing up and go dance with your auntie all that stuff right I think that kind of fluctuated and developed the identity that I kind of built as I was performing here in Australia and we're going to play song from what to say which is Echale Fuego Echale Fuego you are listening to me gente and my people on FBI Radio 94.5 bye

You are listening to Mi Gente, My People on FBi Radio 94.5 and we are joined with Komen Jimenez. Komen, how are you feeling? Yeah, good. Very good. And that's very special. Let's touch on Amaru Tribe. Let the audience know a little bit about the journey, how it started, how did the concept come to life? Well, the process was, through the last years of Watusi, we were touring Melbourne in 2011 or 12. And then in one of those tours, I met my now wife, Catherine. Yes, who's an amazing artist. Yes, amazing visual artist. and then we fell in love and a few months later we decided to stay together and she said why don't you come to Melbourne and I'm like oh okay it's been 12 years in Sydney and I guess maybe I should give it a shot to rediscover Australia and a different city and everybody was telling me about Melbourne and the music scene here so yeah It was a tough decision because, you know, you kind of felt that you build a community in a place and you don't want to leave that. But also, I felt that there was so much for me to learn and to discover. And then when I moved to Melbourne, immediately I started to connect with local artists. There was a very beautiful scene here. There was a band called Lab Jacked and Madre Monte and a bunch of other Latin alternative bands that were kind of really pushing the scene. Yes. So that inspired me also to kind of like to start something new. I was still playing with What You See until 2015. Okay. And during those times, we started doing some demos of music that I had and that I showed to Catherine and she will start, you know, improvising and emceeing. She's a great emcee. She's a great emcee. Because we love hip-hop and stuff. So we ended up recording one of the first tracks, which was called By the Other Soul, has a demo. And then from that, we decided, okay, well, I guess we should start a project together. Beautiful. And it was in 2016 that the first release came about, the official release of The Mother Tribe. Yeah. And that was a six-piece band at that point. And it was more towards, I was trying to not imitate what you see, but really kind of opened myself up to kind of a bit more electronic and experimental with someone more fultronic. I had a very kind of very Latino band. I was most of the band members were Latino background. Yep, yep, yep. So that gave it a different sound. and then through the years the band progressed and we decided to reform in 2019 to give space to the electronic and reduce the project to a four piece and we've been like that since then

You are listening to Mi Gente, My People on FBi Radio 94.5, and we are joined with Carmen Jimenez. Why has it been so important for you to bring in the indigenous or the Afro-Colombian roots within this project? Obviously, it's always been in there, where you're from. You grew up in Barranquilla, which is more present. exactly so a lot of the folklore that i grew up with uh out of those sounds has the gaita which is an indigenous flute at the time the tambor alegre the cumbia sound yeah but not just the cumbia sound but all these carnival rhythms that's so rich and so embedded already naturally in my in my compositions i was already making some of that that fusion with what to see and i felt like i wanted to open a little bit more to get to deepen a little bit more yeah i was watching i was listening to a lot of artists from latin america at that time there was this whole movement of digital cumbia you know you get chancha via circuito and you have nicola cruz and you have and i was like really inspired by those guys i said well i really want to kind of explore that and that's how Amato Tribe became a bit of that exploration but also maintaining a connection with Australia was important as well to say well we're in Australasia there's so many sounds of Asia around here so some of the collaborations we bring about we have a jiraki player Stuart Fergie from Oka rest in peace and a few other artists like from Thailand we had a collaboration with Yuland Yuland Luhan I can't remember the name but they the possibilities just opened up because you're on a different such a exciting and different parts of the world so I said let's explore that let's expand the Latin sounds into this area. I think that's beautiful because with what you say, it's like you're bringing the Latin sounds to the people. So it's like you sharing something that they might not know or like, you know, connecting with the audience in a way where, you know, it's like upbeat and fun and, you know, enjoying. But with this, it's like you're connecting with actually the people from here. So bringing the indigenous cultures together and, you know, making it so that it's not just the Latin music and the fusion of everything other people in Colombia connecting with that they might not know what's in Australia that's right so exporting the music and working with so many amazing artists and you have to do that with a lot of responsibility a lot of these sounds come from ancestral heritage that we're exposed and we try to always acknowledge that in all our shows with Amado Tribe. Beautiful. The sounds that they guide us and those streets of Carnival, they come from Afro-Colombian communities that inspire us and that fusion with us and that brought the Colombian culture you know they elevated the Colombian music culture. Yes. Right? So this is what we're trying to do. It's not to take away from it but actually to bring the light on it yeah it's so beautiful okay man after a decade of creating performing and building community what do you hope the next generation takes from amaru tribe and the work that you've done here in australia i guess that i hope that we you know built a step for them to to put the feet on and continue yeah and to get inspired to get to know the culture as well yes but also value what you have here in australia it's a beautiful country as well that has so much so much to offer and to bring people in you know to bring people in so people get to travel and to uh get to love latin american culture just you know by listening to us listening to the music of course because i actually was inspired by you with what to say thanks man so for me like i didn't really grow up in a latin community but when i didn't get to experience seeing that is i just connected with straight away you know and even the progression of america was another thing you know like and it's so nice to see you know even though yeah we've been doing it for so long it's what we do is actually we're getting even stronger you know getting deeper in how we are and expressing our ways in new in new forms you Yeah, and I think it comes back in other ways. I'm getting inspired by Australian music. I love Australian music where we get to play in different festivals that are not specifically Latin festivals, but I get to play in electronic music festivals and get to other scenes, other acts, you know, like I can number a few, like Hayatus Coyote. and My Life and yeah so many artists and music that you don't unconsciously they're influencing you when you go into the studio some of those sounds translate and if you pay attention to Golden Roots there's a bit of Australian music influences right there Komen, it was a pleasure talking with you today thank you so much and congratulations on 10 years of Amaru Tribe what an achievement not only for the Latin community but the next generation who are finding new ways to connect with their culture their ancestors and their roots thanks hermano I really hope that we get to connect again and yeah let the music continues and grow always and you can get a copy of Golden Roots on vinyl through Bandcamp stream their album online and also we'll be putting up all this information on our socials you're listening to me hand to my people on FBI Radio 94.5.
